cues.text: Let us now turn to metrics and calculations, the part of the subject where we put numbers on how a network behaves.
We start with three terms that people often confuse.
Bandwidth is the nominal capacity of a link, which is the rated maximum it is designed to carry.
Throughput is the actual rate at which data is transferred.
Goodput is narrower still: it excludes protocol overhead and retransmissions, so it counts only the useful data that actually arrives.
So bandwidth is what the link promises, throughput is what you really get, and goodput is the part of that which is genuinely useful to the application.
Next, utilisation.
Utilisation equals the measured bit rate divided by the capacity, multiplied by one hundred percent.
Now, how do we get a measured bit rate from a device?
One common way is SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol, which reports interface counters in octets.
An octet is eight bits.
To turn those counters into a rate, take the difference between two counter readings, multiply it by eight to convert octets into bits, and divide by the number of seconds between the readings.
In symbols, rate equals counter difference times eight, divided by seconds.
Here is the worked example.
Suppose the counter rises by seventy-five million octets in sixty seconds.
Seventy-five million times eight is six hundred million bits, and divided by sixty seconds that gives ten megabits per second.
If this is a one-hundred megabit per second link, utilisation is ten divided by one hundred, which is ten percent.
One practical note: use sixty-four-bit high-capacity counters when appropriate, because on fast links the older, smaller counters can wrap around quickly.
Now let us move on to latency.
Latency is delay, and it is composed of four parts: propagation, transmission, processing and queuing.
Transmission delay, also called serialization delay, equals the packet size in bits divided by the link bit rate.
For example, a packet of one thousand five hundred bytes sent on a ten megabit per second link requires one point two milliseconds to serialise onto the wire.
Propagation delay equals distance divided by signal speed.
For a hundred kilometres of fibre, with a signal speed of roughly two hundred thousand kilometres per second, the one-way propagation delay is approximately zero point five milliseconds.
Round-trip time, or RTT, includes both the forward and the return delays.
Be careful here: do not divide RTT by two to get the one-way delay unless you have assumed that the path is symmetric.
Jitter is the variation in packet delay.
If you want to measure it one way, you need suitable clock synchronisation between the two ends.
Packet loss equals packets sent minus packets received, divided by packets sent, multiplied by one hundred percent.
If twenty out of one thousand packets are lost, the loss is two percent.
One more subtlety: application-level retransmission may mask loss, because the user sees the data arrive, but it does so while increasing latency.
Let us see how these ideas combine in a congestion example.
A one-hundred megabit per second uplink carries eighty-five megabits per second of sustained traffic, plus burst traffic.
Queues grow, RTT rises from twenty milliseconds to one hundred and fifty milliseconds, and voice jitter increases.
This suggests congestion, but you should validate it by checking errors, CPU, duplex, wireless airtime, traffic patterns and the path itself, rather than concluding from one symptom.
This leads us to bufferbloat, which means excessive queue delay.
And it leads us to the idea of a bottleneck, which is the limiting resource.
The important point is that the bottleneck is not always bandwidth.
Server CPU, DNS, storage, the route taken, radio interference or an application dependency may dominate the delay a user experiences.
Finally, how should we measure and judge performance?
Measure a baseline, and also measure peaks and percentiles, for instance the ninety-fifth percentile, or p95, of delay.
Averages alone can hide the bad moments.
Availability equals uptime divided by the observation period, multiplied by one hundred percent.
As an example, ninety-nine point nine percent availability over thirty days permits forty-three point two minutes of unavailability, if the target is defined that way.
For voice, the illustrative targets are often less than one hundred and fifty milliseconds of one-way delay, low jitter of around thirty milliseconds, and low loss of around one percent.
Note that these are illustrative, and the real requirements vary by codec and application.
Video needs sustained throughput and buffering.
Bulk data transfer, by contrast, tolerates delay, but it needs fairness and reliability.
